summary: This program stores a price with cents in a double and then converts it to an int, dropping the decimal part so an advertisement can show a round dollar amount. It prints $100 instead of $100.30.

lines.text: The real selling price needs a type that holds decimals, so it goes in a double.

lines.code: int adPrice = (int) price; // narrow casting from double to int
lines.text: The (int) written in front of price is an explicit cast: because an int cannot hold decimals, Java requires you to state the target type as a way of confirming you accept the loss.

lines.code: int adPrice = (int) price; // narrow casting from double to int
lines.text: Narrowing truncates rather than rounds, so 100.30 becomes 100 — and 100.99 would also become 100, not 101.
Joining the number to a string with + turns it into text for display, which is why the dollar sign can sit right next to the value.
